summary: A Reuters-sourced report republished by Allwork.Space describes growing investor resistance to the wave of corporate debt financing the AI buildout. Fund managers say credit quality at hyperscalers like Amazon and Alphabet remains sound, but the sheer volume of issuance is forcing buyers to demand higher yields, producing what Schroders' Neil Sutherland calls "indigestion" in tech spreads. Tech corporate bonds, historically among the tightest-trading in investment grade credit thanks to strong balance sheets and modest borrowing needs, now trade wider than the broader market. Amazon's recent long-dated $25 billion bond sale priced at roughly 120 basis points over Treasuries, about double the spread it would have carried a year earlier. Capital Group's Karen Choi puts tech spreads at 89 basis points, 9 wider than the overall investment grade market. AI hyperscaler issuance reached $220 billion in 2026 through August 10 per BNP Paribas, versus $12.5 billion in the comparable prior-year period. DWS's George Catrambone says investors now require larger new-issue concessions, citing roughly 10 to 15 basis points on Alphabet's recent offering, and that deals absorbed easily in January now need more yield to clear. He also notes a structural shift: issuers that once borrowed modestly and short-dated are now issuing large volumes of long-term paper, broadening the maturity curve. The surge, alongside heavy government borrowing, has helped push Treasury yields higher; any pullback in tech issuance could support longer-dated Treasuries. Investors are not yet alarmed, pointing to strong ratings, substantial cash flows, and an investment grade index yielding around 5.4%, in line with long-term averages. Foreign investors, pension funds and insurers have absorbed much of the supply. The larger constraint may be portfolio limits: many pension and insurance investors cap single-issuer exposure at roughly 2% to 3% of assets, and clients value diversification. Alphabet declined to comment; Amazon did not respond.
